title: Integrated Planning & Approach Selection
sequence: First topic of the Planning Focus Area. The charter exists; this topic sets the frame (approach, tailoring, delivery strategy) and shows how the plans from Topics 15–23 become one plan. The integration step happens once the component plans exist; the plan then stays alive until Closing.

header.html: Process domain (41%) · Task 1 Develop an integrated project management plan and plan delivery — assess project needs, complexity and magnitude · recommend a development approach (predictive, adaptive/agile or hybrid) · determine critical information requirements (e.g., sustainability) · recommend a project execution strategy · create an integrated project management plan · estimate work effort and resource requirements · assess consolidated project plans for dependencies, gaps and continued business value · maintain the integrated plan · collect and analyze data to make informed project decisions

html:
1Core Concepts and Definitions

Term Meaning
Project management plan The document describing how the project will be executed, monitored and controlled, and closed. It is the basis for all project decisions and a living document that is expected to change. Its content is tailored to the project; it may be high level or detailed
Component (subsidiary) plans The management plans and baselines that together make up the project management plan (see the table below)
Baseline The approved version of a work product that can be changed only through formal change control and is the basis for comparing actual results
Scope / schedule / cost baselines Scope: approved scope statement + WBS + WBS dictionary. Schedule: approved schedule model with baseline start and finish dates. Cost: approved time-phased budget, excluding management reserve
Planning Focus Area The processes that establish the total scope, define and refine objectives, and develop the course of action
Progressive elaboration Iteratively adding detail to the plan as more information and more accurate estimates become available
Rolling wave planning A technique of progressive elaboration: near-term work is planned in detail, later work at a higher level, and decomposed as information arrives
Development approach How the product, service or result is created and evolved: predictive, adaptive or hybrid (Topic 03)
Complexity A characteristic of a project or its environment that is hard to manage because of human behavior, system behavior and ambiguity
Configuration management Procedures that track project artifacts and monitor and control changes to them, so the product, service or result stays consistent and operative
Basis of estimates Supporting documentation showing how an estimate was derived: assumptions, constraints, level of detail, range (e.g., ±10%), confidence level and risks that influence it
Work performance data → information → reports Raw observations → data compared with the plan and thresholds → compiled representations that generate decisions, actions or awareness

What belongs in the plan (PMBOK 8 Section 4):

Group Components
Approach Development approach, project life cycle and tailoring decisions, set at the start and used as input to every performance domain
Management plans Scope · requirements · schedule · financial · quality · resource · communications · stakeholder engagement · risk · sourcing strategy · procurement · change · (configuration management, if applicable)
Adaptive / delivery plans Release plan · iteration plan · test plan
Baselines Scope baseline · schedule baseline · cost baseline

The team or the organization may tailor which components the plan includes (only what is relevant to the context).

Plan versus project documents. The plan says how the work is managed. Project documents record data and status and change constantly: risk register, issue log, assumption log, stakeholder register, change log, lessons learned register, requirements documentation and traceability matrix, milestone list, schedule and communications records. Documents are updated routinely; baselines change only through change control.

Terminology

Watch the PMBOK 8 term: the change management plan sets up the change control board (CCB, also called a steering committee), its authority, and how the change control system works. It is about controlling changes to the project, not about organizational change management (Topic 32).

2The Planning Focus Area: How Much Planning?

  • Planning is progressive, iterative or rolling wave. Detailed planning for work that is far away is wasted effort because information is missing; planning is refined as information arrives.
  • PMBOK 8 rule: the time spent planning, up front and throughout, depends on the circumstances. Planning should give enough information to move forward appropriately, but be no more detailed than necessary. Planning artifacts exist to confirm stakeholder expectations and give stakeholders the information they need to make decisions, take action and stay aligned.
  • Too little planning: misalignment, rework, surprise dependencies. Too much: wasted effort, a plan that is out of date before it is used. Either extreme is a wrong answer.
Approach How planning is shaped
Predictive Plan the whole scope (or each phase) in detail up front; progressive elaboration within phases; changes through change control
Adaptive Brief high-level planning (vision, roadmap), then frequent replanning: release plan → iteration plan → daily coordination; each iteration contains planning, executing and monitoring (Topic 04)
Hybrid Detailed plans for stable or regulated parts; rolling wave or iterative planning for the uncertain parts

3Assess Project Needs, Complexity and Magnitude

This assessment comes before choosing the approach and estimating. It tells you how demanding the project is and what the plan must achieve.

Dimension Questions to answer Typical effect on the plan
Needs What business need and value is the project meant to deliver (business case, benefits)? What do stakeholders need and expect? What are the requirements, and which compliance, security or sustainability needs apply? Drives scope, success measures, priorities, approach
Complexity How hard is it to manage because of people (many parties, cultures, conflicting interests), systems (interdependencies, integrations, new technology) and ambiguity (unclear requirements, uncertain outcomes)? More flexible or phased approaches, more stakeholder work, dependency mapping, prototypes
Magnitude (size and scale) Beyond PMBOK 8ECO wording Budget, duration, team size, number of stakeholders and sites, strategic importance, safety or regulatory criticality More governance and planning rigor, larger reserves, more reporting, PMO involvement

Complexity in more detail (PMBOK 8 glossary and principles):

Source Examples Planning response
Human behavior Many stakeholders with competing interests, distributed or multicultural teams, politics Stakeholder engagement and communication planning, clear governance, team agreements
System behavior Tight interdependencies, many interfaces, new or integrated technology Dependency mapping, modular or incremental delivery, prototypes, a holistic view
Ambiguity Unclear requirements, emerging environment, unknown outcomes Iterative/adaptive approach, rolling wave planning, spikes or prototypes, reserves
  • PMBOK 8 merged the older "navigate complexity" principle into Adopt a Holistic View: for highly complex projects, look at the whole system and its interdependencies, understand them and simplify them. For highly uncertain projects, build techniques into planning to progressively identify and address sources of uncertainty.
  • Size and complexity (Standard §4.3): more flexible approaches suit larger, complex projects with evolving requirements. Tailoring also looks at criticality, scale, duration, standards, culture, number of stakeholders and organizational maturity (Topic 05).
  • How to assess: expert judgment, stakeholder analysis, requirements workshops, comparison with similar projects, a project canvas for a one-page view, prompt lists such as VUCA and PESTLE (Topic 21), and the suitability filter (Topic 05).
Exam angle

assess first. The approach, governance rigor, estimates and reserves are consequences of the assessment, not preferences of the project manager.

4Recommend the Development Approach

Full factor table and definitions are in Topic 03 (section 7); the tailoring process is in Topic 05. The exam-style decision:

Clues in the scenario Likely best fit
Requirements well understood and stable; change is costly (for example the build phase of construction); heavy regulation with phase gates; safety-critical work Predictive
Requirements emerging; high innovation; users available for frequent feedback; value in early partial delivery; funding uncertain Adaptive / agile
Part of the scope is fixed or regulated and part is exploratory; fixed end date with an agile team Hybrid (for example milestones with iterations beneath them)
Scope is well understood but phased delivery pays off because of size, complexity or risk Predictive with incremental delivery (partial value earlier, scope and timeline largely fixed)

Complexity models used in practice [Beyond PMBOK 8 — exam practice]. A Stacey-type graph places a project by how far its requirements are from agreement and how far its technology is from certainty; Cynefin sorts situations by how clearly cause and effect are linked. They lead to the same logic:

Zone Signals Fit
Simple (clear) Requirements agreed, technology proven Predictive; apply known good practice
Complicated One axis is uncertain (proven technology but stakeholders disagree, or the reverse); experts can work out cause and effect Analysis, expert input and structured stakeholder alignment; predictive or incremental with strong planning
Complex Both axes are uncertain; cause and effect are clear only afterwards Experiment in short cycles: adaptive or iterative with fast feedback
Chaotic A crisis; nothing is stable Act to stabilize first, then move to a complex or complicated approach

  • The project manager recommends; the sponsor or governance body approves. Organizational policy or a contract may mandate an approach and limit tailoring.
  • Different deliverables in one project can use different approaches; each team still experiences one way of working.
  • Record the choice (and the reasoning) in the project management plan: it is the first content of the integrated plan and an input to every performance domain.
  • Revisit it when conditions change (retrospectives, phase gates, new information). Tailoring is not a one-time exercise.

5Determine Critical Information Requirements

What it means: deciding early which information the project must produce, collect and receive so that decisions are sound, obligations are met and stakeholders stay aligned. Beyond PMBOK 8as a named activity. PMBOK 8 §2.1.6.2 gives the reason: planning artifacts give stakeholders the information they need to decide, act and stay aligned. The ECO's example is sustainability.

Information requirement Examples Where it lands in the plan
Decisions for sponsor and governance Business case and benefit indicators, cost and schedule variance thresholds, risk exposure, success metrics Governance and escalation thresholds, communications and financial reporting plans
Compliance and regulatory evidence Audit trails, test records, security classification, privacy and safety evidence Quality plan, compliance approach (Topic 23), schedule
Sustainability data (ECO example) Energy and material use, emissions, waste, supplier sustainability performance, social impact; required by regulation, customer or policy Requirements, quality metrics, source selection criteria (PMBOK 8 lists alignment with sustainability goals), risk register, reporting plan, collection tasks in the schedule and budget
Delivery information Standards, interfaces, constraints, assumptions, dependencies Requirements, assumption log, schedule
Stakeholder information needs Who needs what, when and in what form (executive dashboard vs team board) Stakeholder engagement and communications plans

How to determine it:

  1. Ask the sponsor, governance bodies, regulators, customers and teams what they must know, by when and for which decision.
  2. Check contracts, regulations, policies and OPAs for mandatory reporting.
  3. Turn each need into a measurable indicator with a source, owner and frequency.
  4. Build collection into the plans (tasks, budget, tools, roles). Data that is not planned for usually cannot be reconstructed later.
  5. Review the list when conditions change.
Exam angle

identify information requirements during planning (compliance reports, sustainability metrics) and plan their collection. Discovering them at the first report date is the wrong answer.

New requirement after baselining [Beyond PMBOK 8 — exam practice]: if a new critical information requirement appears once the plan is baselined (for example a new duty to report supplier data to a regulator), it changes the baselined plan. Raise it through change control, assess the effect on scope, schedule, cost and resources, and update the affected plans. Adding it quietly to the next status report, or handing it to another department without a decision, leaves the plan inconsistent.

6Recommend an Execution Strategy

What it means: deciding how the project will deliver its outcomes. Beyond PMBOK 8as a single named item. PMBOK 8 spreads the pieces across the Standard (life cycle, development approach, delivery cadence), the Plan Sourcing Strategy process, and governance. It also says the plan may be called a "project execution plan", the document that explains the framework within which decisions are made.

Decision Options Lean toward when
Life cycle and phases Predictive phases with gates, iterative, incremental, hybrid See section 4 and Topic 03
Delivery cadence (Standard §4.4) Single · multiple · periodic (fixed schedule, such as every two weeks) · continuous (always production-ready, automated) Single: value only exists at the end. Multiple/periodic/continuous: early value, feedback, lower risk per release
Release / rollout pattern Beyond PMBOK 8 Big bang · phased by component or region · pilot then rollout · parallel run Phased/pilot/parallel for critical operations or high failure risk; big bang when parts cannot work separately
Sourcing (Plan Sourcing Strategy) Insource (make) · outsource (buy) · mix Make: expertise exists, tighter control or strategic advantage, much innovation needed. Buy: missing expertise, common goods or services, frees capacity, transfers delivery risk (PMBOK 8 Table 2-3). Detail in Topic 22
Delivery solution (ECO, procurement) Build custom · buy off-the-shelf · adapt Buy now and fill the remaining gap in later increments when a product meets most needs and a custom build would delay all value
Governance and team model Structured or self-governing; colocated or remote; dedicated or matrixed Topic 12 and Topic 19
  • Value early and risk small: exam answers favor strategies that deliver value early, learn quickly and avoid one big, irreversible bet.
  • The strategy goes into the plan and must be consistent with the approach, governance model, sourcing strategy and reserves.

7Create the Integrated Project Management Plan

Process (PMBOK 8 Governance domain): Integrate and Align Project Plans.

Aspect Detail
Purpose Integrate, align and coordinate all plan components into one project management plan. The benefit is a thorough document that explains the basis for all project activities and how they will be executed
When Typically once or at specific intervals (for example at each phase), then maintained
Step 1 At the start, establish the overall tailoring considerations and determine the development approach and life cycle; these become part of the plan and input to every domain
Step 2 Bring in all management plans and baselines from the domains and verify their alignment; add the change and configuration management plans where applicable
Content Tailored to the context and complexity; high level or detailed; built to adapt, ideally by progressive elaboration
Format May be called a project governance plan, project management plan, project execution plan, development plan or implementation plan; it must make the decision-making framework transparent to everyone
Key output Project management plan
Decision tools Expert judgment · data gathering (brainstorming, checklists, focus groups, interviews) · interpersonal skills (conflict management, facilitation, meeting management) · meetings · project canvas (one-page view of purpose, objectives, scope, deliverables, approval requirements, assumptions and constraints, milestones, resources, stakeholders, risks, team)
Communication The output is documented and communicated to key stakeholders

What each component plan answers (and where it is covered):

Plan or baseline Question it answers Topic
Scope and requirements management plans; scope baseline How scope and requirements are defined, validated and controlled 15
Schedule management plan; schedule baseline How the schedule is developed, baselined and controlled 16
Financial management plan; cost baseline How costs are estimated, budgeted, funded and controlled; reserves 17
Quality management plan Standards, metrics, assurance and control activities 18
Resource management plan How resources are estimated, acquired, managed and released 19
Communications management plan Who needs what information, when and how 20
Stakeholder engagement plan How stakeholders are engaged and expectations aligned 13
Risk management plan How risk is identified, analyzed, answered and monitored 21
Sourcing strategy and procurement management plans What to make or buy and how to buy it 22
Change and configuration management plans Who approves changes and how artifacts are tracked 29
Release, iteration and test plans Adaptive delivery plans 04, 16, 18
Exam angle

integration is more than stapling plans together. The point is to find and resolve conflicts between plans before baselining and to get the plan understood by the people who must use it.

8Estimate Work Effort and Resource Requirements

(The chart is a study aid showing typical accuracy versus effort; it is not a PMBOK 8 figure.)

8.1 Techniques

Technique How it works Use when Watch out
Expert judgment Judgment from people with relevant expertise Any stage; new or unusual work Bias; combine with data
Analogous (top-down) Uses historical data from a similar activity or project (duration, cost, size, complexity) as a gross value, adjusted for known differences Early, with limited detail; quick and low cost Less accurate; reliable only when the earlier work is similar in fact, not just in appearance, and estimators have the expertise
Parametric An algorithm or statistical relationship between historical data and a variable (e.g., 1,000 m of cable at 25 m per hour = 40 hours) Repeatable work with reliable data Accuracy depends on the model and data behind it
Bottom-up Decompose to lower-level WBS components, estimate each, aggregate Detail is available; setting a baseline Typically the most accurate but needs the most effort and a defined scope
Multipoint (three-point) Uses optimistic (tO), most likely (tM) and pessimistic (tP) values to get an expected value and a range Uncertain activities Needs honest ranges
Relative size (story points, T-shirt sizing) Compares work items instead of predicting hours; story points reflect relative effort or complexity (teams compare better than they predict) Adaptive work, uncertain items Points are team-specific and not hours
Delphi / wideband Delphi, planning poker Estimators give individual estimates, then discuss and repeat until consensus: a diverge/converge pattern that limits groupthink Team estimates, especially agile All three are named in PMBOK 8 (Schedule domain and glossary); know the idea, not the mechanics

The cheaper/faster-but-rougher nature of analogous estimating and the model-dependent accuracy of parametric estimating come from PMBOK 8; ranking bottom-up as the most accurate is common exam practice Beyond PMBOK 8.

8.2 Formulas

Formula Source
Triangular: tE = (tO + tM + tP) / 3 PMBOK 8 (used when historical data are insufficient or judgmental)
Beta / PERT: tE = (tO + 4·tM + tP) / 6 [Beyond PMBOK 8 formula]: PMBOK 8 lists PERT as an estimating technique but prints only the triangular formula; very common on the exam
Standard deviation: SD = (tP − tO) / 6; variance = SD² Beyond PMBOK 8
Range: tE ± 1 SD ≈ 68%, ± 2 SD ≈ 95% Beyond PMBOK 8
Parametric: quantity ÷ rate PMBOK 8 example
Effort vs duration: duration = effort ÷ (number of resources × availability) Beyond PMBOK 8

Worked examples

  • tO = 10, tM = 16, tP = 28 days → PERT tE = (10 + 64 + 28) / 6 = 17 days; SD = (28 − 10) / 6 = 3 days; about 68% probability of finishing between 14 and 20 days. The triangular average would be (10 + 16 + 28) / 3 = 18 days. Use the formula the question names.
  • 120 person-hours of work, 2 people each available 75% → duration = 120 ÷ (2 × 0.75) = 80 hours of elapsed working time.

8.3 Basis of estimates and good practice

  • Basis of estimates: record how the estimate was built: assumptions, constraints, level of detail, range (for example ±10%), confidence level and the individual risks that influence it. The goal is a clear, complete understanding of how the number was derived.
  • Typical early-stage accuracy ranges [Beyond PMBOK 8, older PMBOK terms the exam may still use]: rough order of magnitude (about −25% to +75%), budget estimate (about −10% to +25%), definitive estimate (about −5% to +10%). Ranges narrow as the plan is elaborated.
  • Involve the people who will do the work, use historical data and benchmarks, and refine as information arrives.
  • Estimate all resource types: people, equipment, materials, facilities and tools, not only labor. Effort, duration, cost and resources must be consistent with each other.
  • Padding is not contingency. Hidden safety margins at every level distort the baseline and hide risk. Show assumptions and ranges, and cover uncertainty with an explicit reserve sized from risk analysis (Topics 17 and 21).
  • An estimate is a forecast with a range; a baseline is a commitment that changes only through change control.
  • Adaptive estimating: use relative sizing; forecast using the team's velocity (Topic 16); estimate epics roughly, stories in points and tasks in hours (PMBOK 8 Figure 5-1).
  • AI can propose estimates from historical data and spot patterns; the project manager and team validate them (Topic 08).

9Assess Consolidated Plans: Dependencies, Gaps and Continued Business Value

Run this check on the integrated plan before baselining and whenever the plan changes materially.

Dependencies (PMBOK 8): each dependency has two attributes.

Attribute Meaning
Mandatory (hard logic) Required by law, contract or the nature of the work (foundation before superstructure)
Discretionary (soft or preferred logic) Chosen from good practice or preference; document it, because it limits later options and creates float
Internal Between project activities; the team controls it
External Involves non-project activities or parties (regulator approval, utility connection, another project); the team does not control it, so coordinate and show it in the schedule rather than assume it away

What to cross-check:

Check Typical conflicts
Schedule vs sourcing Lead times and contract dates against the activities that need the items
Schedule vs resources Resource availability, calendars, equipment and shared resources
Cost vs everything Budget phasing against purchase dates and resource profile; reserves against risk
Quality vs schedule Hold points, test and review time, acceptance criteria
Risk vs plans Response actions reflected in schedule, budget and resources
Communications and governance vs schedule Gate reviews, reporting cadence, approval times
Requirements vs scope Every requirement traced to a deliverable and WBS element (traceability matrix)
Assumptions The same assumption used the same way in every plan

Gaps: missing scope or work, missing resource types (equipment and materials), missing roles or approvers, missing acceptance criteria, missing compliance or sustainability work, missing dependencies on other projects or operations, risks without owners or responses.

Continued business value: compare the integrated cost, schedule and benefit picture with the business case and benefits plan and with strategic priorities. If the numbers no longer justify the investment, take the updated figures to the sponsor and governance body with options (rescope, change funding, phase, stop). The decision is theirs.

Resolution rule: when integration reveals a clash, resolve it inside the integrated plan before baselining: adjust the plans, re-verify alignment, re-estimate where needed. Do not just log it as a risk. Where stakeholders hold conflicting or unstated expectations (for example about production impact), surface and agree on them before baselining.

Tools: dependency analysis, schedule network and critical path, requirements traceability matrix, checklists, peer reviews and walkthroughs, project canvas, stakeholder review sessions, and AI-assisted consistency checks (with human review).

10Maintain the Integrated Plan

The plan is a living document (progressive elaboration). Maintain it deliberately:

Trigger Action
Approved change request Update every affected plan, baseline and document; communicate it
Corrective or preventive action Update plans if the action changes how work is done
Performance results and forecasts Re-forecast; replan if the baseline no longer reflects reality (through change control)
Lessons learned, retrospectives, gate reviews Improve the plan, process and approach
New risks, issues, external or organizational change Reassess impact on the plan and on business value (Topics 32, 33)
More information (progressive elaboration, rolling wave) Add detail for the next wave of work
  • Baselines change only through formal change control, even when correcting an error. Documents (registers, logs) are updated routinely. Management plans are revised and re-approved as needed.
  • Configuration management keeps artifacts consistent: identify the items, control versions, record and report changes, verify that the right version is in use.
  • Communicate updates to stakeholders who are affected; an unshared plan update causes misalignment.
  • Adaptive work: the backlog is refined continuously, the roadmap and release plans are adjusted each iteration or release, and changes in priority flow through the backlog and the product owner, not through a change board for every item.
  • Hybrid: the baseline covers the stable envelope (milestones, budget, regulated scope); iteration plans and backlog adapt inside it. A change request is needed only when the envelope changes.

11Collect and Analyze Data to Make Informed Project Decisions

The chain (PMBOK 8 Section 4):

Stage What it is Examples
Work performance data Raw observations and measurements from the work Work completed, actual costs and dates, story points done, defects, number of change requests, KPIs
Work performance information Data compared with the plan, thresholds and context Variances, trends, forecasts; compared with variance thresholds it shows whether corrective or preventive action is needed
Work performance reports Compiled representations to generate decisions, actions or awareness Status and progress reports, EV graphs, burn charts, risk summaries, dashboards

Techniques by purpose:

Purpose Techniques
Gather Brainstorming, interviews, focus groups, questionnaires and surveys, benchmarking, checklists, observation, document analysis
Analyze Variance, trend, regression, earned value, root cause, alternative, cost-benefit, what-if, simulation, sensitivity, SWOT, stakeholder and process analysis
Represent Pie (nominal data), bar (ordinal), histogram (discrete), line (continuous), cause-and-effect and flow diagrams, matrices, dashboards, information radiators
Decide Voting (unanimity, majority, plurality), autocratic, multicriteria decision analysis, decision tree analysis (EMV)

Voting and decision rules (PMBOK 8):

Technique Meaning
Unanimity Everyone agrees on one course of action
Majority More than 50% support (an odd group size avoids ties)
Plurality The largest block decides, even without a majority (useful with more than two options)
Autocratic One person decides for the group
Multicriteria decision analysis A decision matrix with weighted criteria scores and ranks the alternatives

Good decision practice

  • Unilateral decisions are fast but error-prone and can demotivate; group decisions tap more knowledge and build buy-in and commitment but take time. Choose which decisions deserve group discussion.
  • Diverge, then converge: gather options individually first (limits the influence of senior or charismatic voices), then converge. Roman voting, wideband Delphi and fist of five use this pattern and reduce groupthink.
  • The deciding authority (a person or a group) decides on the presented analysis, with stakeholder expectations in mind.
  • Beyond your authority? Escalate with alternatives, impacts and a recommendation ("do not bring me problems, bring me solutions").
  • Pitfalls: unreliable data, vanity metrics, confirmation bias, mistaking correlation for cause. AI can analyze data, but a human stays accountable (Topic 08).
  • [Beyond PMBOK 8] A sound sequence: define the decision and criteria → gather and check the data → generate alternatives → analyze → decide at the right level → communicate and act → review the outcome.

12Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Planning depth Detailed up front for the whole scope or each phase; progressive elaboration within phases Light up front (vision, roadmap, release plan); detailed only for the current iteration; replan each iteration Detailed for fixed or regulated parts; rolling wave for the rest
What "the plan" is Formal project management plan with baselines Product vision, roadmap, release and iteration plans, backlog, working agreements, definition of done Formal envelope (milestones, budget, governance) plus backlog and iteration plans inside it
Estimating Analogous early, then parametric or bottom-up from the WBS; three-point for uncertain work; baseline Relative sizing (story points), velocity forecasts, team-owned estimates; tasks in hours inside an iteration Bottom-up or parametric for fixed work; story points for backlog items
Integration check Cross-plan alignment, then baseline Alignment of backlog, dependencies between teams and release content at each release and iteration Align the two layers: milestones must match what the iterations can deliver
Maintaining Change control for baseline changes Backlog refinement; product owner orders by value; retrospectives Both
Data and decisions Variance vs baseline, earned value Velocity, burn charts, cycle time; decisions in planning, review and retrospective events Both
Beyond PMBOK 8 Timeboxed spikes to reduce estimation uncertainty

13Tailoring and Interactions

  • Tailor the plan to the context: the depth, the list of components and the amount of documentation depend on size, complexity, criticality, regulation, organizational templates (OPAs) and PMO requirements. A small agile project may have a one-page plan; a regulated infrastructure project needs a detailed, controlled set of plans.
  • Governance: the integrated plan records the decision-making framework, thresholds and escalation paths (Topic 12).
  • Stakeholders: involve them in planning to build understanding and ownership; communicate the plan (Topics 13 and 20).
  • Scope, schedule, finance, quality, resources, risk and procurement each contribute a component plan and each is affected when the others change; the integrated plan keeps them consistent.
  • Sustainability and AI: sustainability objectives and data needs belong in the plan (Topic 07); AI can draft and check plans, but humans review for accuracy, bias and confidentiality (Topic 08).

Signs of a healthy integrated plan [Beyond PMBOK 8]: it is approved and baselined; components do not contradict each other; assumptions are explicit; everyone who must use it has seen it; changes are controlled; it is updated when reality changes.

14Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. Resolve cross-plan conflicts inside the integrated plan before baselining. Do not log a known clash as a risk and baseline anyway, and do not re-examine one plan alone.
  2. Baselines change only through change control, even to correct an error.
  3. Assess needs, complexity and magnitude first; then recommend the approach. Choose by project characteristics (requirements stability, innovation, regulation, feedback availability, team, culture), not by habit.
  4. Hybrid is a legitimate answer when parts of the project differ: predictive for the fixed or regulated parts, adaptive for the uncertain ones.
  5. Recommend, get approval, document. The approach and strategy belong in the plan; policy may limit tailoring.
  6. Plan progressively. Do not detail far-off work that lacks information; do not skip planning in predictive work either.
  7. Match the estimating technique to the information available: analogous when detail is scarce but similar history exists; bottom-up when detail exists and a baseline is needed; parametric with reliable data; three-point or relative sizing for uncertainty.
  8. Analogous data must be comparable. Different technology or scale means re-estimate with relevant experts; padding a flawed basis keeps it flawed.
  9. Padding is not contingency. Use visible assumptions, ranges and an explicit risk-based reserve.
  10. Estimates come from or with the people doing the work and are documented in a basis of estimates; include equipment and materials as well as labor.
  11. External dependencies are shown and coordinated, not assumed to follow standard timelines.
  12. Revalidate business value when the plan or environment changes; take the numbers and options to the sponsor and governance. Do not cut quality or risk responses to force a number.
  13. Identify information requirements early (compliance, sustainability, executive reporting) and plan their collection; a new one after baselining goes through change control.
  14. Decisions beyond your authority are escalated with analysis and options; decisions with several criteria use a structured method such as multicriteria analysis.
  15. Hybrid schedules show milestones with iterations beneath; do not convert a backlog into a false-precision Gantt chart, and do not put every iteration change through a change board.
  16. "Change management plan" in PMBOK 8 means the change control board and change control system, not organizational change.

15Exam Q&A

15.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1A department head tells the project manager to reuse the plan and approach of an earlier office-move project for a new multi-country systems integration. What should the project manager do first?

  • AReuse the earlier plan, since a proven approach reduces planning effort and risk
  • BAsk the PMO to select a method before the project's needs are analyzed
  • CAssess its needs, complexity and magnitude, then recommend a fitting approach
  • DChoose the approach the team prefers and update the earlier plan to match
Show the answer

Answer: C. The assessment of needs, complexity and magnitude comes before choosing an approach, and the approach, rigor and estimates follow from it. Reusing an unrelated plan, picking by preference or letting a method be chosen first reverses that order.

S2An adaptive research project has unclear requirements and unknown outcomes, yet the sponsor demands a fully detailed plan for all 24 months. What is the best response?

  • AUse rolling wave planning: detail the near term, refine later work as learning arrives
  • BPlan everything in detail now and treat all later changes as errors to correct
  • CRefuse to plan beyond the next month, as long-term plans cannot be reliable
  • DProduce the full 24-month plan, since sponsors need certainty before they approve funds
Show the answer

Answer: A. Detailed planning of distant work is wasted effort when information is missing, so planning is progressive: near-term work in detail, later work at a higher level, refined as information arrives. A full upfront plan or no long-term plan at all are the two extremes.

S3A task needs 150 person-hours of effort. Two people will work on it, each available 75% of the time. What is the expected elapsed duration?

  • A56 hours, because the effort is first multiplied by the availability figure
  • B100 hours, because 150 divided by two people at 75% availability gives 100
  • C200 hours, because only 75% of one person's time is counted in the total
  • D75 hours, because the 150 hours are simply split between the two people
Show the answer

Answer: B. Duration equals effort divided by the number of resources times their availability: 150 divided by 1.5 gives 100 hours. Ignoring availability gives 75, counting only one person gives 200, and multiplying the effort by availability gives about 56.

S4The sponsor challenges a 450,000 estimate and asks how it was derived, but the project manager has only the final figure. What should have been recorded?

  • AThe basis of estimates: assumptions, constraints, range, confidence and risks
  • BOnly the names of the experts who produced the figure and the date of the estimate
  • CThe approved budget baseline, which replaces the estimate once it exists
  • DA single contingency percentage applied uniformly to the final estimate
Show the answer

Answer: A. A basis of estimates documents how a number was derived: assumptions, constraints, level of detail, range, confidence level and the risks that influence it. Names, a flat contingency percentage or the baseline do not explain the derivation.

S5Each team member adds a private 20% safety margin to their story estimates, and the release forecast looks long yet still slips. What should the project manager do?

  • AAdd a second margin at the project level to protect the already longer schedule
  • BCut every estimate by 20% so that the schedule meets the sponsor's requested date
  • CAccept the margins, since each owner knows the uncertainty of their own task best
  • DRemove hidden padding, show assumptions and ranges, and add an explicit reserve
Show the answer

Answer: D. Hidden padding distorts the baseline and hides risk; uncertainty is shown through assumptions and ranges and covered by an explicit reserve sized from risk analysis. Accepting the margins, cutting them blindly or stacking another one keeps the distortion.

S6The city inspector must approve the reinforcement before concrete can be poured. How should this dependency be classified?

  • ADiscretionary and external, because the inspector's timing is a matter of preference
  • BDiscretionary and internal, because the team could choose a different order of work
  • CMandatory and external, since regulation requires it and the team cannot control it
  • DMandatory and internal, because the team controls when the inspection is requested
Show the answer

Answer: C. A dependency required by law or by the nature of the work is mandatory, and one involving a non-project party such as a regulator is external, so it is coordinated and shown in the schedule. The other combinations misstate either the obligation or who controls it.

S7After the component plans of a hybrid project are integrated, the total cost is 40% above the figure in the business case. What should the project manager do?

  • ABaseline the plan as it stands and explain the difference in the first status report
  • BCut scope across all the plans until the cost matches the business case
  • CAsk each plan owner to reduce their estimates until the totals agree
  • DTake the updated figures and options to the sponsor and governance for a decision
Show the answer

Answer: D. Comparing the integrated plan with the business case checks continued business value, and when the numbers no longer justify the investment the figures go to the sponsor and governance with options such as rescoping or stopping. Baselining anyway, blind cuts or pressure on estimates hides the issue.

S8The customer's regulator will demand an audit trail of test records at acceptance, but the sprint team's definition of done has no item for collecting them. What should the project manager do?

  • AAsk the customer to take responsibility for producing the audit trail
  • BWait for the regulator to specify the format at the time of the audit
  • CReconstruct the records from team memory just before the acceptance date
  • DAdd the collection tasks, tools, roles and budget to the plans now
Show the answer

Answer: D. Critical information requirements are identified during planning and built into the plans as tasks, tools, roles and budget, because data that was not planned for usually cannot be reconstructed later. Reconstructing, waiting or pushing the duty to the customer risks failing acceptance.

S9A city is replacing the software of its 24-hour emergency dispatch center, where a failure would endanger lives. Which rollout pattern is most appropriate?

  • AA single release to all districts timed for the quietest day of the year
  • BA parallel run or pilot, keeping the old system available until the new one is proven
  • CSwitch off the old system on day one to force everyone onto the new one
  • DA big-bang cutover over a weekend to keep the period of disruption short
Show the answer

Answer: B. Critical operations with a high cost of failure call for a pilot, phased or parallel rollout that keeps a fallback until the new system is proven. A big bang, shutting off the old system or a single release to every district bets everything on one event.

S10A company's pricing algorithm is the core of its competitive advantage, and it has the in-house expertise to improve it. Should the project make or buy the new engine?

  • ABuy it, because a vendor's engine will certainly be cheaper than an internal build
  • BMake it in-house, because expertise exists and the capability is a strategic advantage
  • CBuy it, since freeing internal capacity matters more than keeping control of the algorithm
  • DBuy it, because outsourcing always removes the whole delivery risk from the company
Show the answer

Answer: B. Make is favored when expertise exists, tighter control matters or the capability is a strategic advantage, while buy suits missing expertise or common goods. Outsourcing does not remove all risk, a vendor is not always cheaper, and spare capacity does not outweigh strategic control.

S11A nine-member committee must pick one of four vendors, and no vendor is likely to win more than half of the votes. Which decision rule lets the largest block decide?

  • APlurality, where the option with the most votes wins even without a majority
  • BMajority, where more than half of all the votes are needed to win
  • CAutocratic, where one person decides on behalf of the whole group
  • DUnanimity, where every member must agree on a single course of action
Show the answer

Answer: A. Plurality lets the largest block decide even without a majority, which is useful with more than two options. Unanimity and majority both need broader agreement, and an autocratic decision is made by one person.

S12In a hybrid project, milestones and budget are baselined, and the product owner reorders the iteration scope while staying inside those limits. Is a formal change request needed?

  • AYes, because reordering invalidates the schedule baseline until it is reapproved
  • BYes, because every change to scope requires approval from the change control board
  • CNo, because changes inside the baselined envelope flow through the backlog and product owner
  • DNo, because hybrid projects do not need any baselines or change control at all
Show the answer

Answer: C. In a hybrid project the baseline covers the stable envelope, and priority changes inside it flow through the backlog and product owner; a change request is needed only when the envelope itself changes. Requiring a board decision for every change or abandoning baselines both misread the model.

15.2 Recall Q&As

R1What is the project management plan?

Show the answer

The document that describes how the project will be executed, monitored and controlled, and closed. It is the basis for project decisions, is a living document, and is tailored to the project.

R2Which components does a PMBOK 8 project management plan typically have?

Show the answer

Change, communications, financial, iteration, procurement, quality, requirements, release, resource, risk, schedule, scope, sourcing strategy and stakeholder engagement plans and the test plan; plus the baselines, the development approach and life cycle, and (where applicable) the configuration management plan. Content may be tailored.

R3What are the three baselines?

Show the answer

Scope (scope statement, WBS, WBS dictionary), schedule (approved schedule model) and cost (time-phased budget excluding management reserve). They change only through formal change control.

R4How does the plan differ from project documents?

Show the answer

The plan states how work is managed. Documents (risk register, issue log, assumption log, stakeholder register, requirements records) record data and status and are updated routinely; baselines are updated only through change control.

R5Progressive elaboration versus rolling wave planning?

Show the answer

Progressive elaboration is the ongoing increase in detail as information improves. Rolling wave planning is the technique of detailing near-term work and keeping later work at a higher level.

R6How much planning is enough?

Show the answer

Enough to move forward appropriately and to confirm stakeholder expectations and give stakeholders the information to decide and stay aligned, but not more detailed than necessary.

R7What does Integrate and Align Project Plans do first?

Show the answer

It establishes the tailoring considerations and determines the development approach and life cycle, which become part of the plan and guide every performance domain. It then integrates all management plans and baselines and verifies their alignment.

R8Name the common estimating techniques in PMBOK 8.

Show the answer

Expert judgment, analogous, bottom-up, multipoint, parametric and relative size estimation.

R9Give the triangular and PERT formulas.

Show the answer

Triangular tE = (tO + tM + tP) / 3 (PMBOK 8). PERT tE = (tO + 4tM + tP) / 6 with SD = (tP − tO) / 6 [Beyond PMBOK 8].

R10What does the basis of estimates record?

Show the answer

Assumptions, constraints, level of detail, range of possible values (for example ±10%), confidence level and risks that influence the estimate.

R11Work performance data vs information vs reports?

Show the answer

Data are raw observations; information is data compared with the plan, thresholds and context; reports compile information to generate decisions, actions or awareness.

R12Which decision-making techniques does PMBOK 8 list?

Show the answer

Voting (unanimity, majority, plurality), autocratic decision-making and multicriteria decision analysis; decision tree analysis (EMV) supports choices under uncertainty.

R13What are the four delivery cadences?

Show the answer

Single, multiple, periodic and continuous delivery.

R14What are the dependency attributes?

Show the answer

Mandatory or discretionary (hard or soft logic) and internal or external; they combine, for example a mandatory external dependency.
